title: Did you get my message?
goal: Sort out a WhatsApp message from Sēf on the phone: say it hasn't arrived, ask him to send it again, and confirm you've got it
tip: Object endings join the verb: -ni 'me', -ak 'you (m.)', -ich 'you (f.)', -ah 'him, it', -ha 'her, it'. A risāla is feminine, so 'it' is -ha: ṭarrasht-ha 'I sent it', shift-ha 'I saw it'. wiṣlatni 'it reached me' means 'I got it'.
dialogue: Hello? I sent you a message. Have you seen it?
No, I haven't got it. When did you send it?
A little while ago. The address is in it.
Yes, I've got it. I've seen it now.
items: I sent you (something), I've sent it to you (to a man)
you'll also hear masij (مسج), from English 'message'
have you seen it (f.)? (to a man); I saw it, I saw her
to a woman: shiftīha? (شفتيها؟); a masculine thing: shiftah (شفته)
I haven't got it (f.) (lit. it didn't reach me)
a masculine thing: ma wiṣalni (ما وصلني)
I sent it (f.); you sent it (to a man)
to a woman (you sent it): ṭarrashtīha (طرشتيها); a masculine thing: ṭarrashtah (طرشته)
to a woman: ṭarrshīha (طرشيها); a masculine thing: ṭarrshah (طرشه)
did you get it (f.)? (to a man)
to a woman: wiṣlatich? (وصلتج؟); a masculine thing: wiṣalak? (وصلك؟)
see you, I'll see you (to a man)
to a woman: ashūfich (أشوفج); to a group: ashūfkum (أشوفكم)

title: Tell him I'm on my way
goal: Answer Maryam's call when you're running late: ask her to pass a message to the manager and point her to your email
tip: For 'to me, to him', join l- and the ending to the verb: gūl-li 'tell me', gilt-lah 'I told him', gilt-lhum 'I told them', agūl-lich 'I tell you (f.)'. A vowel before an object ending gets long: yabūn + ah → yabūnah 'they want it', shūfi + h → shūfīh 'look at it'.
grammar: Dative l- + ending on verbs: gūl-lah, gilt-lah, agūl-lich
dialogue: Hello, where are you? The manager's asking for you.
في الطريق. قولي له بكون هناك بعد ربع ساعة
fi ṭ-ṭarīg. gūlī-lah bakūn hnāk baʿd rubʿ sāʿa
On my way. Tell him I'll be there in a quarter of an hour.
زين، بقول له. والملف؟ يبونه حق الاجتماع
zēn, bagūl-lah. w il-malaff? yabūnah ḥagg il-ijtimāʿ
OK, I'll tell him. And the file? They want it for the meeting.
I sent you an email last night. Have a look at it.
هيه، لقيته. وقلت لهم، لا تحاتي
hē, ligētah. w gilt-lhum, la tḥāti
Yes, I've found it. And I've told them, don't worry.
Thanks, that's really kind of you.
It was nothing. Don't be late!
items: (he) wants you, (he's) asking for you (to a man)
a feminine thing: yabūnha (يبونها); the -n of -ūn stays before the ending
I told them; you told them (to a man)
to a woman (you told them): giltī-lhum (قلتي لهم)
have a look at it (m.) (to a woman)
I found it (m.), I found him; you found it (to a man)
to a woman (you found it): ligētīh (لقيتيه)
I told him; you told him (to a man)
to a woman (you told him): giltī-lah (قلتي له); I told her: gilt-lha (قلت لها)
thank you, that's very kind of you (to a woman)
to a man: mā gaṣṣart (u12); the reply: mā sawwēna shay
to a woman: la titʼakhkharīn (لا تتأخرين)
culture: The National (2020) lists ṭarrish 'send' among the Emirati words to use in the workplace: ṭarrish-li 'send it to me', ṭarrasht-lah 'I sent it to him'. In young people's speech it often comes mixed with English, as in 'ana ṭarrasht-lak risāla yesterday'.

title: At the phone shop counter
goal: Buy a phone charger from a shop worker: ask if they have one, take it, and say no to the bag and the receipt
tip: A vowel before an ending gets long: tabi → tabīh 'do you want it (m.)?', abi → abīh, ma abīha 'I don't want it (f.)'; after -a it is -āh: ʿaṭa → ʿaṭāh. With 'me' on the verb, 'it' usually goes on iyyā-: ʿaṭni iyyāh 'give it to me' (you may also hear ʿaṭnīh).
grammar: Object endings after a vowel (tabīh, abīha); ʿaṭni iyyāh
dialogue: السلام عليكم. عندك شاحن حق هالتلفون؟
as-salāmu ʿalaykum. ʿindak shāḥin ḥagg hat-tilifōn?
Hello. Have you got a charger for this phone?
وعليكم السلام. هيه، هذا حق هالموبايل. تبيه؟
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. hē, hādha ḥagg hal-mobāyl. tabīh?
Hello. Yes, this one's for this phone. Do you want it?
Yes, I'll have it. How much?
Fifty dirhams. Shall I put it in a bag?
No, thanks. Just give it to me.
You're welcome. And the receipt, do you want it?
items: recognise: you'll hear it in shops; the course word is tilifōn (تلفون)
do you want it (m.)? (to a man)
to a woman: tabīnah? (تبينه؟); a feminine thing: tabīha? (تبيها؟)
I want it (m.), I'll have it
I put it; shall I put it…?
give it (m.) to me (to a man)
to a woman: ʿaṭīni iyyāh (عطيني إياه); a feminine thing: ʿaṭni iyyāha (عطني إياها)
the receipt, the bill (in a shop)
I don't want it (f.), I don't need it
a masculine thing: ma abīh (ما أبيه)

title: Did you see the photo?
goal: Tell Sēf and the guys where you put the photo from the desert trip, and promise to send them the video
tip: A vowel before an ending gets long: shiftu 'you (pl.) saw' → shiftūha 'you saw it', shifna 'we saw' → shifnāha 'we saw it'. 'To you all' is -lkum: baṭarrish-lkum 'I'll send you'. To a group, the imperative ends in -ū before the ending: shūfūha 'look at it'.
grammar: Object endings with groups: shiftūha, shifnāha, -lkum
dialogue: Guys, where's the photo from the desert?
I put it in the group. Haven't you seen it?
No, we haven't. Where is it?
In the uni group. Have a look at it now.
هيه، لقيناها! ما شاء الله، حلوة
hē, ligēnāha! mā shāʼ allāh, ḥilwa
Yes, we've found it! Wow, it's lovely.
And tomorrow I'll send you the video too.
items: I put it (f.); you put it (to a man)
to a woman (you put it): ḥaṭṭētīha (حطيتيها); a masculine thing: ḥaṭṭētah (حطيته)
haven't you seen it (f.)? (to a group)
to one man: ma shift-ha?; to one woman: ma shiftīha?
a masculine thing: ma shifnāh (ما شفناه)
where is it (f.)? where is she?
where is it (m.), where is he?: wēnah? (وينه؟)
to one man: shūf-ha (شوفها); to one woman: shūfīha (شوفيها)
we found it (f.), we found her
to one man: baṭarrish-lak (بطرش لك); to one woman: baṭarrish-lich (بطرش لج)
we'll see it, we'll watch it (m.)

title: Meet Fahad from Kuwait
goal: Meet Fahad, Sēf's Kuwaiti friend: understand his Kuwaiti 'yes', 'what' and 'not', and ask how long he's staying
tip: Fahad speaks Kuwaiti. Three words to catch: ēh 'yes' (close to your ī from u2), shinu 'what' (UAE shu), and mū 'not' (UAE mub): mū awwal marra 'it's not the first time'. Learn to understand them, and keep using your own shu, mub, ī and hē.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms for recognition: ēh, shinu, mū
dialogue: السلام عليكم. أنا فهد، من ربع سيف
as-salāmu ʿalaykum. ana Fahad, min rabʿ Sēf
Hello. I'm Fahad, one of Sēf's mates.
وعليكم السلام. هلا والله! انت كويتي؟
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. hala wallāh! inta kwēti?
Hello! Great to meet you. Are you Kuwaiti?
ēh, kwēti. w inta shinu ismak?
Yes, Kuwaiti. And what's your name?
اسمي سالم. أول مرة في دبي؟
ismi Sālim. awwal marra fi Dbayy?
My name's Sālim. Is this your first time in Dubai?
لا، مو أول مرة. أحب دبي وايد
la, mū awwal marra. aḥibb Dbayy wāyid
No, it's not my first time. I love Dubai.
Nice! How many days are you staying?
Two weeks. What have you got on tomorrow?
items: like ī (إي) from u2; UAE: hē (هيه)
UAE: shu (شو); shinu ismak? = what's your name?
not (before anything that isn't a verb) (Kuwait)
a woman: kwētiyya (كويتية); the country: il-Kwēt (الكويت)
Kuwait: mū awwal marra = UAE: mub awwal marra (it's not the first time)
will you stay? you'll stay (to a man)
culture: Gulf Arabic is one family with national marks. In dialect novels, Emirati writers use shu about ten times as often as shinu, and Kuwaiti writers do the reverse; Kuwaiti writing also strongly prefers mū to mub. You don't need to switch: recognise Fahad's forms and keep your own.

title: These are my mates
goal: Meet Fahad's friends from Kuwait: catch iḥna, hadhōl and ḥēl, welcome the group and suggest dinner
tip: Fahad says iḥna for 'we' (UAE niḥin) and hadhōl for 'these' (UAE hādhēla). ḥēl means 'very, a lot' and goes before or after the word: ḥēl ḥilu, fikra ḥilwa ḥēl. Kuwaitis say wāyid too. To the whole group, use -ūn and -īn: tabūn 'do you want?', sāknīn.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms for recognition: iḥna, hadhōl, ḥēl
dialogue: سالم، تعال! هذول ربعي من الكويت. تعرفهم؟
Sālim, taʿāl! hadhōl rabʿi min il-Kwēt. tiʿarfhum?
Sālim, come here! These are my mates from Kuwait. Do you know them?
لا، ما أعرفهم. هلا والله، حياكم الله في دبي
la, ma aʿarfhum. hala wallāh, ḥayyākum allāh fi Dbayy
No, I don't. Hi, welcome to Dubai, all of you.
الله يحييك. إحنا هني في إجازة، أسبوعين بس
allāh yḥayyīk. iḥna hni fi ijāza, usbūʿēn bas
Thank you. We're here on holiday, just for two weeks.
Where are you staying? In a hotel?
إيه، في ديرة. حيل حلو، وقريب من كل شي
ēh, fi Dēra. ḥēl ḥilu, w garīb min kill shay
Yes, in Deira. It's really nice, and close to everything.
Do you want to have dinner together tonight?
Oh yes! That's a really good idea.
items: before or after the word: ḥēl ḥilu, fikra ḥilwa ḥēl; UAE: wāyid (وايد)

title: Is there a table?
goal: Wait for Sēf with Fahad at a busy restaurant: understand aku and māku, and find somewhere to sit
tip: Kuwaitis say aku 'there is' and māku 'there isn't' where Emiratis say fī and ma fī: māku ṭāwla 'there are no tables'. shaku? 'what's up?' comes from the same word. Fahad also says mū mushkila for your mub mushkila, and illaḥīn beside il-ḥīn.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms for recognition: aku, māku, shaku
dialogue: He's got work, he'll be a bit late.
مو مشكلة. بس اللحين المطعم زحمة، ماكو طاولة
mū mushkila. bas illaḥīn il-maṭʿam zaḥma, māku ṭāwla
No problem. But right now the restaurant's packed, there are no tables.
إيه، أكو! بس الجو حار برا
ēh, aku! bas il-jaww ḥārr barra
Oh yes, there is! But it's hot outside.
That's fine. Shall we sit outside?
يلا. وقول له إحنا برا، عشان يشوفنا
yalla. w gūl-lah iḥna barra, ʿashān yshūfna
OK. And tell him we're outside, so he can see us.
items: Kuwaitis also say il-ḥīn (الحين), the UAE default

title: Fahad calls home
goal: Talk to Fahad while he phones his parents in Kuwait: catch yumma, yuba, ihu and ihi, and send your greetings
tip: Fahad calls his mother yumma and his father yuba (Kuwait); you'll hear yumma in the UAE too. For 'he' and 'she' he says ihu and ihi (UAE huwa, hiya). Greetings use the endings: sallim ʿalēha 'say hi to her', and the reply allāh ysallimha 'God keep her'.
grammar: Kuwaiti forms for recognition: yumma, yuba, ihu, ihi
dialogue: هلا يمه! إيه، أنا ويا سالم
hala yumma! ēh, ana wiyya Sālim
(on the phone) Hi, Mum! Yes, I'm with Sālim.
Is that your mum? Say hi to her from me.
يمه، سالم يسلم عليج. اهي تسلّم عليك
yumma, Sālim ysallim ʿalēch. ihi tsallim ʿalēk
(on the phone) Mum, Sālim says hi. (to you) She says hi to you.
allāh ysallimha. w ubūk? ʿasāh b-khēr
God keep her. And your dad? I hope he's well.
He's fine, thank God. He's right next to her now.
Great. Say hi to him too.
(on the phone) Dad! Sālim says hi.
items: Mum! (calling or talking to your mother) (Kuwait)
talking about her: ummi (أمي); you'll hear yumma in the UAE too; UAE also: ummāya (أمايه); spelt like yammah (يمه) 'next to him'
Dad! (calling or talking to your father) (Kuwait)
talking about him: ubūy (أبوي); UAE also: ubūya (أبويه)
to a woman: ummich (أمج); your dad: ubūk (أبوك)
say hi to her (from me) (to a man)
to a woman: sallmi ʿalēha (سلمي عليها)
(she) says hi to you (to a man)
to a woman: tsallim ʿalēch (تسلّم عليج); not tislam (تسلم, 'thank you')
God keep her (reply when she sends greetings)
of a woman: ʿasāha b-khēr (عساها بخير)
culture: Inside Kuwait, saying y for j marks urban (ḥaẓar) speech: the Kuwait Times quotes Kuwaiti linguist Rashaid saying Bedouin (badu) speakers don't have it. Even so, Kuwaiti novels write jīt (جيت) more often than yīt (ييت), so expect j from many Kuwaitis where Emiratis say y.
